lessons.title: What Microsoft Sentinel Actually Is

slots.practicalActivity: Sign up for a free Azure account (or use an existing subscription) and, in the Azure Portal, create a new resource group dedicated to this course's labs. Then write two short paragraphs: one contrasting cloud-native pay-as-you-go pricing with an on-prem SIEM's up-front hardware cost, and one explaining in your own words why bundling SIEM and SOAR into a single product (instead of a separate SOAR tool bolted on afterward) is a real architectural choice, not marketing language.
slots.deliverable: A new Azure resource group created for this course's labs, plus two written paragraphs: one contrasting cloud-native pay-as-you-go pricing with on-prem SIEM economics, one explaining why Sentinel bundles SIEM and SOAR into one product.

lessons.title: The Log Analytics Workspace as Sentinel's Foundation

slots.practicalActivity: In your lab resource group, create a real Log Analytics workspace in the Azure Portal (Create a resource -> Log Analytics workspace), noting its name, resource group, and region. From Microsoft Sentinel's own page, enable Sentinel on top of that exact workspace. Then open the workspace's own Overview page, separate from Sentinel's UI, and screenshot its Access control (IAM) blade to confirm it's a distinct Azure resource with its own permissions.
slots.deliverable: A real Log Analytics workspace created in your lab resource group with Sentinel enabled on top of it, plus a screenshot of the workspace's own IAM/Access control blade confirming it exists as a separate Azure resource.

lessons.title: Data Connectors: Bringing Logs into Sentinel

slots.practicalActivity: In your Sentinel workspace's Data connectors gallery, open one connector from each of the three types covered: a service-to-service connector (Microsoft Entra ID), an agent-based connector (Windows Security Events via the Azure Monitor Agent), and an API-based connector (AWS CloudTrail/S3). For each, read its connection instructions and write one sentence describing exactly what full configuration would require. Actually connect the Microsoft Entra ID connector if your tenant allows it, since it's a free, service-to-service connector.
slots.deliverable: Three connector setup pages reviewed (one per connector type) with one written sentence each on what full configuration requires, plus the Microsoft Entra ID connector actually connected and showing a real status if your tenant permits it.

lessons.title: Sentinel Pricing and Data Retention Concepts

slots.practicalActivity: In your workspace's "Usage and estimated costs" page, review the real pay-as-you-go pricing shown. Open the workspace's retention settings and note the free interactive retention window, then use the pricing page's own per-GB numbers to calculate what one additional year of retention would cost for a hypothetical 5 GB/day ingestion workspace. Write one sentence recommending pay-as-you-go vs. a commitment tier for that same hypothetical workspace.
slots.deliverable: A written cost calculation for one extra year of retention at a hypothetical 5 GB/day ingestion rate using your workspace's real pricing page numbers, plus a one-sentence pay-as-you-go-vs-commitment-tier recommendation.

lessons.title: What KQL Is and How It Differs from SQL

slots.practicalActivity: In your Sentinel workspace's Logs page, run the lesson's real KQL query (SigninLogs | where ResultType != "0" | project UserPrincipalName, ResultType) against SigninLogs, or against one of the Logs page's built-in sample queries if your tenant has no real sign-in volume yet. Separately, write out the equivalent SQL SELECT/FROM/WHERE version in a text file, and write one sentence confirming whether KQL's case-sensitive != behaved as the lesson described.
slots.deliverable: A real KQL query run successfully in your workspace's Logs page returning UserPrincipalName and ResultType, plus the same request written out as SQL for comparison and one written note confirming KQL's case-sensitivity behavior.

lessons.title: Basic KQL Queries: Filtering and Projecting

slots.practicalActivity: Against SigninLogs (or a sample dataset if your workspace has little real sign-in volume), write and run three queries building on each other: one with two stacked where clauses (a time window plus a failure filter), one adding a project narrowing to 5 named columns, and one adding take 50. Run the take 50 version twice in a row and compare the two result sets to confirm the sample it returns is arbitrary, not a fixed top-50.
slots.deliverable: Three working KQL queries run in your Logs page (stacked where, +project, +take 50), plus a written note comparing two separate take 50 runs confirming the returned rows are an arbitrary sample, not a ranked list.

lessons.title: Summarizing and Aggregating with KQL

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's FailedSignIns = count() by UserPrincipalName query against your workspace (or sample data), sorted descending. Then write and run a second query using dcount(IPAddress) by UserPrincipalName over the last 7 days. Identify the single highest DistinctIPs value in your results and write one sentence judging whether it would warrant investigation.
slots.deliverable: Two working summarize queries (count() by user, dcount(IPAddress) by user) run against real or sample data, with the highest DistinctIPs result identified and one written sentence judging whether it looks suspicious.

lessons.title: Joining Tables and Time Windows in KQL

slots.practicalActivity: Write and run the full join kind=inner query from the lesson, joining SigninLogs to ThreatIntelligenceIndicator on $left.IPAddress == $right.NetworkIP. Use ago(7d) instead of ago(24h) on both sides if your workspace's threat intel feed or sign-in volume is sparse, so you have a realistic chance of a match. If zero rows return, write one sentence explaining why a legitimate zero-match result is still meaningful, not a broken query.
slots.deliverable: A working join kind=inner query correlating SigninLogs against ThreatIntelligenceIndicator run in your Logs page, plus one written sentence interpreting either a real match or a legitimate zero-match result.

lessons.title: Scheduled Analytics Rules in Sentinel

slots.practicalActivity: In Sentinel's Configuration -> Analytics -> Create -> Scheduled query rule, open the rule-creation wizard and build a draft: paste any KQL query from this chapter's lessons, set "Run query every" to 1 hour and "Lookup data from the last" to 2 hours, and write one sentence explaining why you deliberately set the lookback window longer than the run frequency, per the lesson's ingestion-delay reasoning.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of a draft Scheduled Analytics Rule's "Set rule logic" tab showing a real KQL query, a 1-hour run frequency, and a 2-hour lookback window, plus one written sentence justifying the gap between them.

lessons.title: Built-In vs. Custom Analytics Rules

slots.practicalActivity: Browse Sentinel's Analytics -> Rule templates gallery and find one template tied to a connector you enabled in Chapter 1 (e.g. a Microsoft Entra ID sign-in template). Note its pre-filled query, schedule, and severity. Then open the blank custom-rule wizard and write two sentences: one describing what the template already did for you, one describing what you'd have to write yourself for a rule watching something specific to a fictional company (e.g. "alert if the finance app's custom log table is queried after 10pm").
slots.deliverable: One built-in rule template's pre-filled query, schedule, and severity documented, plus two written sentences contrasting it with what a custom rule for a fictional org-specific scenario would require you to build yourself.

lessons.title: Entity Mapping and Incident Correlation

slots.practicalActivity: Open any analytics rule (a template or your own draft) to its "Set rule logic" tab's Entity mapping section and configure a real mapping: map a column like UserPrincipalName to the Account entity type with identifier FullName, and IPAddress to the IP entity type with identifier Address. Save it as a draft or customized template and screenshot the saved entity mapping configuration.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of a real analytics rule's Entity mapping section showing at least one Account entity (mapped from UserPrincipalName) and one IP entity (mapped from IPAddress) correctly configured.

lessons.title: Writing a Real KQL-Based Detection Rule

slots.practicalActivity: Build the full sequence-aware brute-force-then-success query from the lesson step by step in your Logs page: first run the count-only version (summarize FailedCount = count() by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated,10m) | where FailedCount > 5), reason through a case it would wrongly flag, then build and run the full let Failures / let Successes / join kind=inner version against your workspace or sample data.
slots.deliverable: Both KQL versions run successfully in your Logs page -- the count-only query and the full let/summarize/join sequence-aware version -- with a written sentence identifying a realistic case the count-only version would have wrongly flagged.

lessons.title: What a Sentinel Workbook Actually Does

slots.practicalActivity: In your Sentinel workspace, open Threat Management -> Workbooks and click into any one built-in workbook, even with sparse data. Identify and screenshot one real text step, one real query step, and one real parameter step inside it, labeling each by role. Change the parameter's value (e.g. a time range) and observe which query steps visibly re-run and update.
slots.deliverable: Screenshots of a real built-in workbook's text, query, and parameter steps labeled by role, plus a written note confirming which query step(s) re-ran after you changed the parameter's value.

lessons.title: Built-In Workbooks vs. Custom Dashboards

slots.practicalActivity: In the Workbooks -> Templates gallery, find and activate (Save) one built-in workbook template tied to a connector you enabled in Chapter 1 (Azure AD Sign-in Logs or Office 365). Confirm it now appears in your own Workbooks list. Then write one paragraph proposing a custom workbook combining that same data with one fictional org-specific element (e.g. a hardcoded list of VIP accounts) that no built-in template could have anticipated.
slots.deliverable: One built-in workbook template actually activated and showing in your personal Workbooks list, plus a written paragraph proposing a custom workbook combining that data with one org-specific element.

lessons.title: Visualizing KQL Query Results

slots.practicalActivity: In the Logs page, take a failed-sign-in query and run it three times ending in three different render lines: render timechart on summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated,1h), and render barchart plus render piechart on summarize count() by ResultType. Screenshot each chart and write one sentence on which render type actually fit its data's shape and which looked wrong.
slots.deliverable: Three screenshots of KQL queries rendered as timechart, barchart, and piechart, plus a written sentence identifying which render type didn't fit its data's shape and why.

lessons.title: Building a Workbook for a Specific Use Case

slots.practicalActivity: Build a real custom workbook from scratch in Threat Management -> Workbooks -> New: add a text step describing its purpose, a query step running the failed-login timechart query with a TargetUser parameter substituted in via {TargetUser}, and a parameter step defining TargetUser as a text/dropdown control. Save the workbook with a real name and test it by entering a real or sample username and confirming the chart updates.
slots.deliverable: A saved, named custom workbook with a working text step, a parameterized query step referencing {TargetUser}, and a parameter step -- tested by entering a value and confirming the chart filters to it.

lessons.title: What Defender XDR Actually Unifies

slots.practicalActivity: Navigate to security.microsoft.com (the unified Microsoft Defender portal) and open the Incidents & alerts page. Screenshot it and identify where the four workload names -- Defender for Endpoint, Office 365, Identity, Cloud Apps -- would appear as alert sources. Then write out, in your own words, the full phishing-to-endpoint attack chain from the lesson, naming which Defender workload would catch each of the four steps.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the Microsoft Defender portal's Incidents & alerts page, plus a written four-step walkthrough of the phishing-to-endpoint attack chain naming the Defender workload responsible for catching each step.

lessons.title: Defender for Endpoint Concepts, Revisited in XDR Context

slots.practicalActivity: In Microsoft Sentinel's Data connectors gallery, open the Microsoft Defender XDR (or Microsoft 365 Defender) connector's details page and read exactly what it ingests. If your tenant allows it, enable the connector and in Sentinel's Logs page run a simple query against one of its real tables (e.g. DeviceLogonEvents | take 10 or AlertInfo | take 10) to confirm the schema exists, even with sparse data.
slots.deliverable: The Microsoft Defender XDR data connector's ingestion details documented, plus a KQL query run against a real Defender XDR table name (DeviceLogonEvents, AlertInfo, or AlertEvidence) in your Sentinel workspace's Logs page.

lessons.title: Defender for Office 365 and Email Threat Protection

slots.practicalActivity: In the Microsoft Defender portal, open Email & collaboration -> Policies & rules -> Threat policies and view the real Safe Links and Safe Attachments policy pages (reviewing settings only, without changing a production tenant). Write one paragraph explaining why a Business Email Compromise attempt would pass through both Safe Links and Safe Attachments completely undetected, and which policy type is actually responsible for catching it.
slots.deliverable: Safe Links and Safe Attachments policy pages reviewed in the Defender portal, plus a written paragraph explaining why BEC bypasses both and which policy (anti-phishing/impersonation) actually catches it.

lessons.title: Defender for Identity and Detecting On-Prem AD Attacks

slots.practicalActivity: Research Defender for Identity's sensor requirements (what it needs installed on a domain controller) using Microsoft's own documentation, since this workload requires on-prem AD infrastructure most student labs won't have. Then write a paragraph explaining, in your own words, Pass-the-Hash, Golden Ticket, and DCSync, naming for each the specific observable anomaly Defender for Identity's sensor would actually use to catch it.
slots.deliverable: A written paragraph explaining Pass-the-Hash, Golden Ticket, and DCSync, naming the specific observable anomaly Defender for Identity's domain-controller sensor would use to catch each one.

lessons.title: The Sentinel Incident Queue and Severity Triage

slots.practicalActivity: Open your Sentinel workspace's Incidents page. If you have zero real incidents, briefly enable one of your Chapter 3 analytics rules (or a template) to generate at least one test incident. Sort the queue by severity, note the Status field for your incident, assign it to yourself, and move its status from New to Active.
slots.deliverable: At least one real incident visible in your Sentinel Incidents page, sorted by severity, with its status changed from New to Active and assigned to yourself.

lessons.title: The Investigation Graph and Entity Timelines

slots.practicalActivity: Open the incident from the previous session and click into its investigation graph. Screenshot the graph showing the incident node connected to its mapped entities. Click one entity node to open its entity timeline and screenshot that too. Write one sentence on what the timeline showed that the graph alone did not.
slots.deliverable: Screenshots of a real incident's investigation graph and one entity's timeline, plus one written sentence identifying what the timeline revealed beyond what the graph itself showed.

lessons.title: Hunting Queries and Proactive Threat Hunting

slots.practicalActivity: In Sentinel's Threat Management -> Hunting page, browse the built-in hunting query gallery and run three queries from different tactic categories (e.g. credential access, lateral movement, persistence) against your workspace. Write one sentence interpreting one query's results. Then write and run your own simple custom hunting query answering a question no gallery query covers (e.g. "which users signed in from more than 2 distinct IPs this week").
slots.deliverable: Three built-in hunting queries run from the gallery across different tactics, plus one original custom hunting query you wrote yourself, with a written interpretation of one gallery query's results.

lessons.title: Bookmarks and Building a Case During an Investigation

slots.practicalActivity: From one of the hunting query results in the previous session, select a row and save it as a bookmark. Pin that bookmark to the incident from the Lesson 21/22 sessions. Open the incident again and confirm the bookmark now appears attached to it. Repeat with a second query result so the incident has at least two pinned bookmarks forming the start of a real case file.
slots.deliverable: A real incident with at least two pinned bookmarks attached, each saved from a different query result, confirmed visible on the incident's own page.

lessons.title: Sentinel Playbooks and Azure Logic Apps

slots.practicalActivity: In the Azure Portal, create a real (even minimal) Logic App resource and open it in the Logic Apps designer. Add the Microsoft Sentinel connector's "When a Microsoft Sentinel incident is created or updated" trigger as the first step, then add one simple action after it (e.g. a Teams "Post a message" action, or an "Initialize variable" action if no Teams connection is available). Save the Logic App.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure Logic App created and saved with a Microsoft Sentinel connector trigger as its first step and at least one action configured after it.

lessons.title: Triggering a Playbook from an Incident

slots.practicalActivity: In Sentinel's Configuration -> Automation page, create a real automation rule: set its trigger to "When incident is created," add one condition (e.g. Severity equals Medium or High), and set its action to run the Logic App/playbook you built in the previous session. Save the rule and screenshot its trigger, condition, and action configuration.
slots.deliverable: A saved automation rule in your Sentinel workspace showing a real trigger ("When incident is created"), at least one condition, and an action set to run your playbook from the previous session.

lessons.title: A Real Automation Rule Plus Playbook Example

slots.practicalActivity: Walk through the lesson's phishing-report scenario against your own setup: write out, step by step, what your automation rule's condition would need to check to only match phishing-report incidents (by analytics rule name), and what your playbook's 3 actions would do in sequence (get incident details, notify, tag). If your rule/playbook pair from the last two sessions is working, trigger a test run and confirm in the Logic App's run history that it executed.
slots.deliverable: A written step-by-step walkthrough mapping the phishing-report scenario's condition and 3 playbook actions onto your own rule/playbook, plus, if available, a Logic App run-history entry confirming a real test execution.

lessons.title: When to Automate vs. When to Keep a Human in the Loop

slots.practicalActivity: Sort the lesson's own check-yourself list -- "send a Slack message," "revoke a user's active sessions," "look up a device's last sign-in location" -- into "safe to automate" vs. "needs human approval," writing one justifying sentence each. Then review your own playbook from the last two sessions and write whether every action in it is actually safe to fully automate under this lesson's test, or whether one should have an approval step added.
slots.deliverable: Three actions sorted into safe-to-automate vs. needs-approval with a justifying sentence each, plus a written review of your own playbook's actions against the same safe/needs-approval test.

lessons.title: Lab: Writing a Custom Analytics Rule with KQL
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: End-to-End Detection and Response in Sentinel

slots.practicalActivity: Build the full impossible-travel detection from scratch in your workspace: write and run the self-join KQL query exactly as shown (adjusting ResultType filters to your real or sample data), wrap it in a new scheduled analytics rule with a 1-hour run frequency and 1-hour lookback, and configure entity mapping for both the Account column and the two IP address columns. Save the rule as a real, enabled rule in your workspace.
slots.deliverable: A real, saved, and enabled scheduled analytics rule in your Sentinel workspace implementing the impossible-travel self-join query, with entity mapping configured for the Account and both IP columns.

lessons.title: Lab: Investigating an Incident End to End
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: End-to-End Detection and Response in Sentinel

slots.practicalActivity: If your previous session's rule produced a real incident (or using a test/sample one), work it end to end: open it from the queue, read its investigation graph and the Account entity's timeline, then run the hunting query from the lesson scoped to the incident's own two IP addresses to check for broader compromise, and bookmark the hunting query's result, pinned to the incident.
slots.deliverable: One incident worked end to end -- graph and timeline reviewed, a scoped hunting query run against its two flagged IPs, and the hunting result bookmarked and pinned to the incident.

lessons.title: Case Study: From Raw Logs to Closed Incident
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: End-to-End Detection and Response in Sentinel

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the full 9:14 AM to 9:48 AM case-study timeline from the lesson in your own words as a mock incident report, then write your own closing note for it in the same four-sentence style the lesson modeled (what happened, what the automation did, what the hunting query confirmed, what remediation is still required). Compare your closing note against the lesson's own to check you included all four elements.
slots.deliverable: A written mock incident report covering the full phishing-to-impossible-travel case study, plus an original 4-sentence closing note following the lesson's format (event, automated action, hunting confirmation, remediation required).

lessons.title: Chapter Capstone: Sentinel, Defender XDR & KQL Review
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: End-to-End Detection and Response in Sentinel

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own chapter-by-chapter recap of this entire course in your own words (one or two sentences per chapter, all 8 chapters), explicitly naming which lesson from the last three sessions each chapter's technique shows up in. Then answer the lesson's own closing question in writing: which single chapter would have been hardest to remove from the Lesson 31 case study, and what specifically would the investigation have missed without it.
slots.deliverable: A written 8-chapter recap of the full course tying each chapter to where it showed up in the capstone labs, plus a written answer naming the hardest chapter to remove and what would have broken without it.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can work inside a real Microsoft Sentinel deployment as a working analyst -- writing original KQL queries against Log Analytics tables, building and tuning scheduled analytics rules with entity mapping, creating workbooks that visualize live detections, and reading an incident's investigation graph and entity timeline to scope an attack. They understand how Microsoft Defender XDR's four workloads (Endpoint, Office 365, Identity, Cloud Apps) correlate into one incident, can design and wire up a Logic Apps playbook with an automation rule that reacts to real incidents, and know which response actions are safe to automate versus which need a human approval step. They've personally built a self-join KQL detection rule for impossible travel from scratch, investigated the incident it created end to end with hunting queries and bookmarks, and written a defensible closing note for a multi-stage phishing-to-account-compromise case -- the same detection-and-response loop a real Sentinel SOC analyst runs every day.
